items.text: A Wayne County homeowner reports a wind claim to her insurer on March 1. Under MCL 500.2006(3), by what date must the insurer specify in writing what documents count as a satisfactory proof of loss, unless the claim is settled first?

D. March 31 — MCL 500.2006(3) requires the insurer to specify in writing the materials constituting satisfactory proof of loss not later than 30 days after receipt of the claim, which makes March 31 the deadline here.

An insured under her own homeowners policy waits 75 days after satisfactory proof of loss for payment. The insurer claims the amount owed was genuinely disputed. Does the 'reasonably in dispute' defense in MCL 500.2006(4) apply to her?

B. No, that defense sits only in the second sentence of subsection (4), covering third party tort claimants — MCL 500.2006(4)'s reasonably-in-dispute language appears only in the sentence governing third party tort claimants; the insured's own claim under the first sentence carries no such qualifier.
For a third party tort claimant to collect 12% interest under MCL 500.2006(4), what must be shown in addition to late payment?

C. That the insurer's liability was not reasonably in dispute, the insurer refused payment in bad faith, and a court determined that bad faith — The second sentence of MCL 500.2006(4) requires all three elements for a third party tort claimant: liability not reasonably in dispute, bad-faith refusal, and a court finding of that bad faith.
An insurer offers $50,000 to settle a claim. The claimant rejects the offer and later recovers only $45,000. Under MCL 500.2006(4), is interest due?

A. No, because the claimant did not recover more than the amount offered — MCL 500.2006(4) provides that if payment is offered and rejected, and the claimant does not subsequently recover more than the amount offered, interest is not due.
MCL 500.2026(1)'s preamble requires unfair practices to be, other than isolated incidents, what kind of conduct?

B. A course of conduct indicating a persistent tendency to engage in that type of conduct — The statute's preamble requires 'a course of conduct indicating a persistent tendency to engage in that type of conduct,' not a single isolated incident.
An adjuster tells a homeowner a fire loss is excluded when the exclusion does not actually apply to the facts. Which MCL 500.2026(1) subsection does this most directly violate?

B. (a), misrepresenting pertinent facts or policy provisions relating to coverages at issue — Subsection (a) covers misrepresenting pertinent facts or insurance policy provisions relating to coverages at issue, which fits telling an insured an exclusion applies when it does not.
An insurer denies a claim without ever inspecting the property or reviewing the homeowner's documentation. Which MCL 500.2026(1) subsection is squarely on point?

D. (d), refusing to pay claims without conducting a reasonable investigation based on available information — Subsection (d) targets refusing to pay claims without conducting a reasonable investigation based on the available information, which is exactly a desk denial with no inspection.

An insurer pays the clearly-covered dwelling portion of a claim late, on purpose, hoping to pressure the homeowner into accepting a lowball number on the disputed personal-property portion. Which MCL 500.2026(1) subsection fits?

C. (m), failing to promptly settle one portion of a claim to influence settlement of other portions — Subsection (m) covers failing to promptly settle claims where liability has become reasonably clear under one portion of the policy coverage in order to influence settlements under other portions.
A denial letter reads only, 'Your claim is denied. Not covered under the policy,' with no cited provision or fact. Which MCL 500.2026(1) subsection does this violate?

C. (n), failing to promptly provide a reasonable explanation of the basis for denial — Subsection (n) requires a reasonable explanation of the basis in the policy, in relation to the facts or law, for a denial or compromise offer; a bare 'not covered' letter fails that.
Under MCL 500.2026(2), what must an insurer keep about complaints received since its last DIFS examination?

A. A complete record showing total number, classification by line, nature, disposition, and processing time — MCL 500.2026(2) requires a complete complaint record with total number, classification by line of insurance, nature, disposition, and processing time; failing to keep it is itself a violation.
Under MCL 500.2028, on what basis may the commissioner investigate an insurer's affairs for unfair practices?
B. Probable cause — MCL 500.2028 authorizes examination and investigation 'upon probable cause' to determine whether unfair methods of competition or deceptive acts have occurred.
Before a formal notice of hearing issues under MCL 500.2029, what must bureau staff first offer the person under investigation?

C. An opportunity to confer and discuss the matter informally, with possible summary disposition — MCL 500.2029 requires bureau staff to give the person an opportunity to confer and discuss the possible complaint informally before a notice of hearing issues, and the matter may be resolved summarily by agreement.
At a Chapter 20 hearing under MCL 500.2030, who carries the burden of proof?

B. The agency (DIFS), or an intervenor opposing the person under investigation — MCL 500.2030(2) places the burden of proof at the hearing on the agency, or upon an intervenor who intervened in opposition to the person subject to the proceeding.
DIFS finds an insurer committed 4 Chapter 20 violations, and did not know and had no reason to know it was violating the chapter. Under MCL 500.2038(1)(a), what is the maximum total monetary penalty?

D. $4,000, at $1,000 each, capped by the $10,000 aggregate — For ordinary, non-knowing violations, the penalty is not more than $1,000 per violation, not to exceed a $10,000 aggregate; 4 violations at $1,000 each totals $4,000, under the cap.
After a cease-and-desist order is already in effect, an insurer violates it again. Under MCL 500.2040(1)(a), what is the maximum monetary penalty per violation?
C. $20,000 — MCL 500.2040(1)(a) sets the penalty for violating a live cease-and-desist order at not more than $20,000 for each violation, in addition to possible license suspension or revocation.
A restoration contractor tells a homeowner that Kewin v Massachusetts Mutual lets them sue the insurer in tort for mental-distress damages over a delayed claim. Is this accurate?

A. No, Kewin declined to make bad-faith breach of an insurance contract an independent, separately actionable tort — Kewin's holding declined to declare mere bad-faith breach of an insurance indemnity contract an independent and separately actionable tort; no first-party bad-faith tort exists in Michigan, and Nickola (a different subject, penalty interest) did not overrule it.
A public adjuster describes the phrase 'wholly separate and independent duty' as a direct quote from the Kewin opinion. Is that accurate?

D. No, that exact phrase does not appear in the Kewin opinion text; Kewin's own words refuse to make bad-faith breach 'an independent and separately actionable tort' — A full-text check of the Kewin opinion this run found no instance of 'wholly separate and independent.' The verified Kewin quote is that the Court declined to make bad-faith breach an independent and separately actionable tort.

A liability insurer refuses a within-limits settlement offer, never tells its insured about the offer, and an excess judgment results. Under Commercial Union v Liberty Mutual, what is the governing standard for the insurer's exposure to the excess judgment?

A. Arbitrary, reckless, indifferent, or intentional disregard of the interests of the person owed a duty — Commercial Union defines third-party bad faith, for jury-instruction purposes, as arbitrary, reckless, indifferent, or intentional disregard of the interests of the person owed a duty, and lists 12 non-exclusive factors including failing to inform the insured of settlement offers and rejecting reasonable within-limits offers.

A homeowner sues their insurer under the Michigan Consumer Protection Act today, alleging conduct that would also violate MCL 500.2026. Citing Smith v Globe Life (1999), they argue the claim survives. What is the correct current-law answer?

A. Incorrect, MCL 445.904(3) now bars an MCPA claim resting on Chapter 20 conduct occurring on or after March 28, 2001 — Smith v Globe Life applied the 1999-era statute, which then allowed the claim to proceed. The Legislature closed that door; MCL 445.904(3) now bars MCPA claims resting on Chapter 20 conduct for anything occurring on or after March 28, 2001.
A public adjuster tells a client that Michigan now has a statutory bad-faith lawsuit against insurers because of Senate Bill 245. What is the correct answer as of this check?

D. Incorrect, SB 245 is still pending: it would add a Chapter 30B private cause of action, but it was only reported from committee and referred to the Committee of the Whole — SB 245's proposed Chapter 30B would create a private civil cause of action against insurers for violations of MCL 500.2006, 500.2026, and 500.2027, but the bill was only reported favorably without amendment June 17, 2026, and referred to the Committee of the Whole June 18, 2026. It has not passed either chamber, so none of it is law.
